Premier League Match Outcome Prediction¶

Background¶

Can you predict Premier League results from public data alone? I took three seasons of match data (2023/24 through 2025/26), built form and travel features that only use past matches, and tested eight models against the Bet365 betting market. The market is the benchmark here. It prices matches with data I do not have, like injuries and lineups, so the honest question is how close a model built on public history can get.

Setup¶

The notebook downloads raw match data from football-data.co.uk at runtime: three seasons (2324, 2425, 2526), 1130 matches, from 2023-08-11 to 2026-05-19. That means it needs an internet connection and the packages in requirements.txt to run as is. The heavy part is the model tuning and the LSTM, which take a long time.

The repo also holds the finished feature set. epl_features_2324.csv is the saved output of the feature engineering step: 1130 rows with the 12 final features (the name is a leftover; it covers all three seasons, not just 2324). The notebook itself rebuilds everything from the live download and does not read these CSVs.

Method¶

Getting the data¶

Three seasons of Premier League results plus in-game stats (shots, shots on target, corners, fouls) and Bet365 odds for every match.

First look at the data¶

Home teams win 43.2% of the time, away teams 32.4%, draws 24.4%. Home teams average 1.62 goals per game versus 1.38 for away teams, and they outshoot the visitors 14.3 to 11.8. Shots on target track goals closely, which is no surprise: you cannot score without them.

None of the in-game stats are predictive by themselves, since they are only known after the final whistle. But they motivate the features: rolling form has to come from past matches only.

Goals follow a Poisson pattern¶

Goal counts sit close to a Poisson distribution, with lambda 1.62 for home teams and 1.38 for away teams. That is the justification for modeling each team's expected goals as a Poisson rate later.

In [6]:

The betting market as a baseline¶

Bet365 odds imply probabilities. After removing the bookmaker margin, those probabilities are very well calibrated: when the market says 60%, the outcome lands about 60% of the time. Shot dominance also lines up with results in the obvious way: outshoot the opponent and you usually win.

That sets the bar. The market's log-loss is 0.9639, and raw accuracy is not the right way to compare models against it. A model that is right 50% of the time with honest probabilities beats one that is right 52% of the time while overconfident. So every model here is scored on log-loss under walk-forward time-series cross-validation: train on the past, predict the future, five folds.

In [7]:
df["Shot_Diff"] = df["HS"] - df["AS"]
df["Home_Win"]  = (df["FTR"] == "H").astype(int)

bins    = pd.qcut(df["Shot_Diff"], q=10, duplicates="drop")
prob_df = df.groupby(bins, observed=True)["Home_Win"].mean().reset_index()
prob_df["Bin_Center"] = prob_df["Shot_Diff"].apply(lambda x: x.mid).astype(float)

# Compute normalised bookmaker probabilities
df["Overround"] = 1/df["B365H"] + 1/df["B365D"] + 1/df["B365A"]
df["Prob_H"] = (1/df["B365H"]) / df["Overround"]
df["Prob_D"] = (1/df["B365D"]) / df["Overround"]
df["Prob_A"] = (1/df["B365A"]) / df["Overround"]
df["Actual_H"] = (df["FTR"] == "H").astype(int)
df["Actual_D"] = (df["FTR"] == "D").astype(int)
df["Actual_A"] = (df["FTR"] == "A").astype(int)

y = df["FTR"].map({"A": 0, "D": 1, "H": 2}).astype(int)
market_loss = log_loss(
    y, np.column_stack([df["Prob_A"], df["Prob_D"], df["Prob_H"]]), labels=LABELS
)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 6))

axes[0].scatter(prob_df["Bin_Center"], prob_df["Home_Win"], s=100, color="royalblue")
axes[0].axhline(0.5, color="gray", linestyle="--")
axes[0].axvline(0,   color="gray", linestyle="--")
axes[0].set_title("Empirical Win Probability vs. Shot Difference")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Shot Dominance (Home Shots - Away Shots)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("P(Home Win)")

axes[1].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k:", label="Perfectly Calibrated")
for probs_col, actuals_col, label, color, marker in [
    ("Prob_H", "Actual_H", "Home Win (Bet365)", "blue",  "s"),
    ("Prob_A", "Actual_A", "Away Win (Bet365)", "red",   "^"),
    ("Prob_D", "Actual_D", "Draw (Bet365)",     "green", "o"),
]:
    fp, mp = calibration_curve(df[actuals_col], df[probs_col], n_bins=10)
    axes[1].plot(mp, fp, f"{marker}-", color=color, label=label)

axes[1].set_title("Reliability Diagram: Betting Market Calibration")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Mean Predicted Probability (Bet365 Implied)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Fraction of Actual Outcomes (Empirical)")
axes[1].legend(loc="upper left")
axes[1].set_xlim(-0.05, 1.05)
axes[1].set_ylim(-0.05, 1.05)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"Bet365 market log-loss: {market_loss:.4f}")

A team-level example: rolling form¶

Features need to summarize how a team has been playing, using only matches already played. Here is Manchester City across the three seasons: the five-game rolling average of shots for and against. The gap between those lines is a rough measure of dominance, and it moves a lot over a season.

In [8]:
TARGET_TEAM = "Man City"   # change to any team in the dataset

tm = df[(df["HomeTeam"] == TARGET_TEAM) | (df["AwayTeam"] == TARGET_TEAM)].copy()
tm["Team_Scored"]   = np.where(tm["HomeTeam"] == TARGET_TEAM, tm["FTHG"], tm["FTAG"])
tm["Team_Conceded"] = np.where(tm["HomeTeam"] == TARGET_TEAM, tm["FTAG"], tm["FTHG"])
tm["Team_Shots"]    = np.where(tm["HomeTeam"] == TARGET_TEAM, tm["HS"],   tm["AS"])
tm["Opp_Shots"]     = np.where(tm["HomeTeam"] == TARGET_TEAM, tm["AS"],   tm["HS"])
tm = tm.reset_index(drop=True)
tm["Match_No"]           = tm.index + 1
tm["Rolling_Shots"]      = tm["Team_Shots"].rolling(WINDOW, min_periods=1).mean()
tm["Rolling_Opp_Shots"]  = tm["Opp_Shots"].rolling(WINDOW, min_periods=1).mean()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 5))

sns.kdeplot(data=tm["Team_Scored"],   fill=True, label="Goals Scored",   ax=axes[0])
sns.kdeplot(data=tm["Team_Conceded"], fill=True, label="Goals Conceded", ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title(f"{TARGET_TEAM}: Goals Scored vs. Conceded")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Goals per Match")
axes[0].legend()

axes[1].plot(tm["Match_No"], tm["Rolling_Shots"],    label=f"{TARGET_TEAM} Shots ({WINDOW}-game avg)")
axes[1].plot(tm["Match_No"], tm["Rolling_Opp_Shots"],label=f"Opponent Shots ({WINDOW}-game avg)")
axes[1].fill_between(tm["Match_No"],
                     tm["Rolling_Shots"], tm["Rolling_Opp_Shots"], alpha=0.15)
axes[1].set_title(f"{TARGET_TEAM}: Attacking vs. Defensive Volatility")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Match Number (Chronological)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Number of Shots")
axes[1].legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This rolling window is the core idea. Every feature below is computed the same way: only past matches, shifted so the current match never leaks in.

Feature engineering¶

Twelve features per match, all leakage-free. For each team: five-game rolling averages of goals scored, shots on target, and points; venue-split expanding averages of goals and shots on target at home (for the home team) and away (for the away team); and a travel fatigue number, the cumulative miles traveled over the last five matches computed from stadium GPS coordinates. The venue split matters because teams play differently at home. The shift(1) in the code makes sure the current match is never included.

In [9]:
# ── Stadium GPS coordinates ───────────────────────────────────────
STADIUM_COORDS = {
    "Arsenal":          (51.5549, -0.1084),
    "Aston Villa":      (52.5092, -1.8847),
    "Bournemouth":      (50.7352, -1.8380),

    "Crystal Palace":   (51.3983, -0.0855),
    "Everton":          (53.4388, -2.9664),
    "Fulham":           (51.4749, -0.2217),
    "Ipswich":          (52.0536,  1.1444),
    "Leeds":            (53.7778, -1.5737),

# ── Helper functions ─────────────────────────────────────────────
def haversine_miles(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2):
    lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2 = map(radians, [lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2])
    a = sin((lat2 - lat1) / 2)**2 + cos(lat1) * cos(lat2) * sin((lon2 - lon1) / 2)**2
    return 3958.8 * 2 * atan2(sqrt(a), sqrt(1 - a))


def build_team_log(df):
    """Reshape wide match data to one row per team per match."""
    home = df[["Date", "HomeTeam", "AwayTeam", "FTHG", "FTAG", "FTR", "HST", "AST"]].copy()
    home.columns = ["Date", "Team", "Opponent", "GF", "GA", "FTR", "SOT_F", "SOT_A"]
    home["Venue"]  = "H"
    home["Points"] = home["FTR"].map({"H": 3, "D": 1, "A": 0})

    away = df[["Date", "AwayTeam", "HomeTeam", "FTAG", "FTHG", "FTR", "AST", "HST"]].copy()
    away.columns = ["Date", "Team", "Opponent", "GF", "GA", "FTR", "SOT_F", "SOT_A"]
    away["Venue"]  = "A"
    away["Points"] = away["FTR"].map({"A": 3, "D": 1, "H": 0})

    return (
        pd.concat([home, away], ignore_index=True)
        .sort_values(["Team", "Date"])
        .reset_index(drop=True)
    )


def venue_expanding_mean(group_df, venue_flag, col):
    """
    Leakage-free expanding average restricted to one venue type.
    Rows at the wrong venue become NaN; expanding().mean() skips them.
    Shift(1) ensures the current match is never included.
    """
    mask = group_df["Venue"] == venue_flag
    return (
        group_df[col]
        .where(mask)
        .expanding()
        .mean()
        .shift(1)
        .fillna(0)
    )


def compute_travel_fatigue(group_df, team_name):
    """Cumulative travel miles over the last WINDOW matches (leakage-free)."""
    if team_name not in STADIUM_COORDS:
        return pd.Series(0.0, index=group_df.index)

    hlat, hlon = STADIUM_COORDS[team_name]
    prev_lat, prev_lon = hlat, hlon
    dists = []

    for _, row in group_df.iterrows():
        clat, clon = (
            (hlat, hlon)
            if row["Venue"] == "H"
            else STADIUM_COORDS.get(row["Opponent"], (hlat, hlon))
        )
        dists.append(haversine_miles(prev_lat, prev_lon, clat, clon))
        prev_lat, prev_lon = clat, clon

    return (
        pd.Series(dists, index=group_df.index)
        .shift(1)
        .rolling(WINDOW, min_periods=1)
        .sum()
        .fillna(0)
    )


# ── Build team log ───────────────────────────────────────────────
print("Building per-team match log...")
team_log = build_team_log(df)
grp = team_log.groupby("Team")

# ── Overall rolling form (leakage-free via shift inside transform) ──
print("Computing rolling form...")
team_log["Roll_GF_5"]  = grp["GF"].transform(
    lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(WINDOW, min_periods=1).mean().fillna(0))
team_log["Roll_SOT_5"] = grp["SOT_F"].transform(
    lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(WINDOW, min_periods=1).mean().fillna(0))
team_log["Roll_Pts_5"] = grp["Points"].transform(
    lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(WINDOW, min_periods=1).sum().fillna(0))

# ── Venue-specific expanding form (loop avoids pandas apply index issues) ──
print("Computing venue-specific form...")
for col_out, venue_flag, col_in in [
    ("Home_GF_Form",  "H", "GF"),
    ("Home_SOT_Form", "H", "SOT_F"),
    ("Away_GF_Form",  "A", "GF"),
    ("Away_SOT_Form", "A", "SOT_F"),
]:
    team_log[col_out] = 0.0
    for team, g in team_log.groupby("Team"):
        team_log.loc[g.index, col_out] = venue_expanding_mean(g, venue_flag, col_in).values

# ── Travel fatigue ────────────────────────────────────────────────
print("Computing travel fatigue...")
team_log["Travel_Fatigue_5"] = 0.0
for team, g in team_log.groupby("Team"):
    team_log.loc[g.index, "Travel_Fatigue_5"] = compute_travel_fatigue(g, team).values

# ── Merge features back to match level ───────────────────────────
print("Merging to match level...")
FEAT_COLS = [
    "Date", "Team",
    "Roll_GF_5", "Roll_SOT_5", "Roll_Pts_5",
    "Home_GF_Form", "Home_SOT_Form",
    "Away_GF_Form", "Away_SOT_Form",
    "Travel_Fatigue_5",
]

home_feats = (
    team_log[team_log["Venue"] == "H"][FEAT_COLS]
    .rename(columns={"Team": "HomeTeam",
                     **{c: f"H_{c}" for c in FEAT_COLS if c not in ("Date", "Team")}})
)
away_feats = (
    team_log[team_log["Venue"] == "A"][FEAT_COLS]
    .rename(columns={"Team": "AwayTeam",
                     **{c: f"A_{c}" for c in FEAT_COLS if c not in ("Date", "Team")}})
)

df = df.merge(home_feats, on=["Date", "HomeTeam"], how="left")
df = df.merge(away_feats, on=["Date", "AwayTeam"], how="left")

# ── Final feature list & target ───────────────────────────────────
FEATURES = [
    "H_Roll_GF_5",  "H_Roll_SOT_5",  "H_Home_GF_Form",  "H_Home_SOT_Form",
    "H_Roll_Pts_5", "H_Travel_Fatigue_5",
    "A_Roll_GF_5",  "A_Roll_SOT_5",  "A_Away_GF_Form",  "A_Away_SOT_Form",
    "A_Roll_Pts_5", "A_Travel_Fatigue_5",
]

X = df[FEATURES].fillna(0)
y = df["FTR"].map({"A": 0, "D": 1, "H": 2}).astype(int)
N_FEAT = X.shape[1]   # 12

print(f"\nFeature matrix : {X.shape}")
print(f"Target counts  :\n{y.value_counts().sort_index().rename({0:'Away',1:'Draw',2:'Home'})}")
print("\n--- Feature Summary ---")
print(X.describe().round(3).loc[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]])

The models¶

Eight approaches, all scored the same way. Six standard classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, an MLP), each tuned with a small grid search inside a pipeline with a standard scaler. Then a Poisson regression that predicts each team's expected goals and turns the two rates into win/draw/away probabilities through the bivariate Poisson table. Then an LSTM over the 12 features. And the Bet365 market as the baseline to beat.

Two implementation notes from the code: logistic regression uses the saga solver because lbfgs threw overflow warnings on this data, and the LSTM treats each match as a single timestep rather than a true sequence of past matches (a real sequential setup would feed a window of prior matches).

In [10]:
# Note: solver='saga' replaces 'lbfgs' for LogisticRegression — 'lbfgs' was
# producing hundreds of divide-by-zero/overflow warnings from sklearn's matmul
# on this dataset. 'saga' is numerically more stable for multiclass problems.
#
# Note on LSTM architecture: input_shape=(1, N_FEAT) treats each match as a
# single timestep. This replicates the original design. True sequential
# modelling would pass a sliding window of prior matches as the time dimension.

BASE_MODELS = {
    "1. Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(
        solver="saga", max_iter=2000, random_state=SEED),
    "2. Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(random_state=SEED),
    "3. Gradient Boosting": GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=SEED),
    "4. XGBoost": XGBClassifier(
        objective="multi:softprob", eval_metric="mlogloss",
        random_state=SEED, verbosity=0),
    "5. LightGBM": LGBMClassifier(random_state=SEED, verbose=-1),
    "6. Neural Network (MLP)": MLPClassifier(
        solver="adam", max_iter=500, early_stopping=True, random_state=SEED),
}

PARAM_GRIDS = {
    "1. Logistic Regression": {
        "model__C":       [0.01, 0.1, 1.0],
        "model__penalty": ["l2"],
    },
    "2. Random Forest": {

    },

        "model__num_leaves":    [31, 63],
    },
    "6. Neural Network (MLP)": {
        "model__hidden_layer_sizes": [(32,), (64, 32)],
        "model__alpha":              [0.001, 0.01],
    },
}


def build_lstm(n_features):
    """Build and compile the LSTM used throughout this notebook."""
    model = Sequential([
        LSTM(32, input_shape=(1, n_features), activation="relu"),
        Dropout(0.2),
        Dense(16, activation="relu"),
        Dense(3,  activation="softmax"),
    ])
    model.compile(loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", optimizer="adam")
    return model


print("Model definitions ready.")

Model definitions ready.

Training and walk-forward evaluation¶

This cell does the heavy lifting: grid search for the six classifiers, then five-fold walk-forward evaluation for every model. Walk-forward means a model only ever trains on earlier matches and predicts later ones, which is how it would actually be used. The LSTM trains 40 epochs per fold. It takes a while; the results below are the curated outputs.

In [11]:
# ── Hyperparameter tuning ─────────────────────────────────────────
print("--- Hyperparameter Tuning ---\n")
tuned_models = {}
for name, base_model in BASE_MODELS.items():
    pipe = Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler()), ("model", base_model)])
    grid = GridSearchCV(
        estimator=pipe, param_grid=PARAM_GRIDS[name],
        cv=TSCV, scoring="neg_log_loss", n_jobs=-1, refit=True,
    )
    grid.fit(X, y)
    tuned_models[name] = grid.best_estimator_
    print(f"[{name}]  best log-loss: {-grid.best_score_:.4f}")

# ── Walk-forward evaluation ───────────────────────────────────────
print("\n--- Walk-Forward Evaluation ---\n")
results = {}
poisson_y_true, poisson_y_prob = [], []  # Saved for Poisson confusion matrix & calibration

# 1. Standard sklearn models
for name, pipe in tuned_models.items():
    f_logloss, f_acc, f_f1 = [], [], []
    for train_idx, test_idx in TSCV.split(X):
        pipe.fit(X.iloc[train_idx], y.iloc[train_idx])
        probs = pipe.predict_proba(X.iloc[test_idx])
        preds = np.argmax(probs, axis=1)
        y_test = y.iloc[test_idx]
        
        f_logloss.append(log_loss(y_test, probs, labels=LABELS))
        f_acc.append(accuracy_score(y_test, preds))
        f_f1.append(f1_score(y_test, preds, average='macro'))
        
    results[name] = {'Log-Loss': np.mean(f_logloss), 'Accuracy': np.mean(f_acc), 'F1-Macro': np.mean(f_f1)}

# 2. Poisson regression
f_logloss, f_acc, f_f1 = [], [], []
for train_idx, test_idx in TSCV.split(X):
    sc = StandardScaler()
    X_tr, X_te = sc.fit_transform(X.iloc[train_idx]), sc.transform(X.iloc[test_idx])

    pr_h = PoissonRegressor(alpha=0.1, max_iter=1000).fit(X_tr, df["FTHG"].iloc[train_idx])
    pr_a = PoissonRegressor(alpha=0.1, max_iter=1000).fit(X_tr, df["FTAG"].iloc[train_idx])

    probs = np.zeros((len(test_idx), 3))
    for i, (lh, la) in enumerate(zip(pr_h.predict(X_te), pr_a.predict(X_te))):
        lh, la = max(float(lh), 1e-6), max(float(la), 1e-6)
        ph, pd_tie, pa = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
        for h in range(10):
            for a in range(10):
                ps = poisson.pmf(h, lh) * poisson.pmf(a, la)
                if h > a:    ph      += ps
                elif h == a: pd_tie += ps
                else:        pa      += ps
        tot = ph + pd_tie + pa
        probs[i] = [pa / tot, pd_tie / tot, ph / tot]
        
    preds = np.argmax(probs, axis=1)
    y_test = y.iloc[test_idx]
    
    f_logloss.append(log_loss(y_test, probs, labels=LABELS))
    f_acc.append(accuracy_score(y_test, preds))
    f_f1.append(f1_score(y_test, preds, average='macro'))
    
    poisson_y_true.extend(y_test.tolist())
    poisson_y_prob.extend(probs.tolist())

results["7. Poisson Regression"] = {'Log-Loss': np.mean(f_logloss), 'Accuracy': np.mean(f_acc), 'F1-Macro': np.mean(f_f1)}

# 3. RNN (LSTM)
f_logloss, f_acc, f_f1 = [], [], []
for train_idx, test_idx in TSCV.split(X):
    sc = StandardScaler()
    X_tr = sc.fit_transform(X.iloc[train_idx]).reshape(-1, 1, N_FEAT)
    X_te = sc.transform(X.iloc[test_idx]).reshape(-1, 1, N_FEAT)

    lstm = build_lstm(N_FEAT)
    lstm.fit(X_tr, y.iloc[train_idx], epochs=40, batch_size=16, verbose=0)

    probs = lstm.predict(X_te, verbose=0)
    preds = np.argmax(probs, axis=1)
    y_test = y.iloc[test_idx]
    
    f_logloss.append(log_loss(y_test, probs, labels=LABELS))
    f_acc.append(accuracy_score(y_test, preds))
    f_f1.append(f1_score(y_test, preds, average='macro'))

results["8. RNN (LSTM)"] = {'Log-Loss': np.mean(f_logloss), 'Accuracy': np.mean(f_acc), 'F1-Macro': np.mean(f_f1)}

# 4. Market Baseline
m_preds = np.argmax(np.column_stack([df["Prob_A"], df["Prob_D"], df["Prob_H"]]), axis=1)
results["Bet365 (Baseline)"] = {
    'Log-Loss': market_loss, 
    'Accuracy': accuracy_score(y, m_preds), 
    'F1-Macro': f1_score(y, m_preds, average='macro')
}

# ── Print ranking ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
print(f"\n{'Model':<30} | {'Log-Loss ↓':<10} | {'Accuracy ↑':<10} | {'F1-Macro ↑':<10}")
print("-" * 68)
# Sort models by Log-Loss (lowest is best)
for name, metrics in sorted(results.items(), key=lambda x: x[1]['Log-Loss']):
    marker = " <--" if "Bet365" in name else ""
    print(f"{name:<30} | {metrics['Log-Loss']:.4f}     | {metrics['Accuracy']:.4f}     | {metrics['F1-Macro']:.4f}{marker}")

The simplest models win. Poisson regression comes closest to the market at 1.0250, with logistic regression right behind at 1.0269. The complex models do worse: gradient boosting and LightGBM overfit the noise in past results and fall short on future matches. None of them beat the market's 0.9639. That is not a modeling failure so much as a fact about the data: public match history does not contain everything the market prices in, like injuries, lineups, and motivation.

Venue-split form carries the most weight. How a team scores at home predicts home goals (+0.115); how the away team creates shots on target on the road predicts away goals (+0.074). Travel fatigue barely registers, which is its own finding: at Premier League distances, the miles do not move the needle much.

Calibration and confusion matrix¶

The confusion matrix has a telling hole: the model never predicts a draw. The draw column is all zeros. Poisson rates for two teams rarely tie exactly, so the model always leans one way. Across the 940 out-of-sample test predictions it gets 50.4% right, which beats the naive always-pick-home baseline of 43.2%. The calibration plot is the better news: when the model says 60% for a home win, it lands near 60%. The probabilities are honest even where they are not sharp.

For the top teams the model and the market agree almost exactly: Man City 64.8% versus 64.5%. The disagreements sit at the bottom of the table. The model gives Sunderland a 42.1% home chance against Chelsea; the market says 26.4%. That is where the model's blindness shows: it only sees past results, not who is injured or who has stopped trying in May.

    {"HomeTeam": "Man City",       "AwayTeam": "Aston Villa"},
    {"HomeTeam": "Brighton",       "AwayTeam": "Man United"},
    {"HomeTeam": "Fulham",         "AwayTeam": "Newcastle"},

    {"HomeTeam": "Crystal Palace", "AwayTeam": "Arsenal"},

def get_latest_features(team: str, is_home: bool) -> dict:
    """Return the most recent rolling features for a team from team_log."""
    hist = team_log[team_log["Team"] == team].tail(1)
    p  = "H_"    if is_home else "A_"
    vp = "Home_" if is_home else "Away_"
    zeros = {
        f"{p}Roll_GF_5": 0.0, f"{p}Roll_SOT_5": 0.0, f"{p}Roll_Pts_5": 0.0,
        f"{p}{vp}GF_Form": 0.0, f"{p}{vp}SOT_Form": 0.0,
        f"{p}Travel_Fatigue_5": 0.0,
    }
    if hist.empty:
        return zeros
    r = hist.iloc[0]
    return {
        f"{p}Roll_GF_5":        r["Roll_GF_5"],
        f"{p}Roll_SOT_5":       r["Roll_SOT_5"],
        f"{p}Roll_Pts_5":       r["Roll_Pts_5"],
        f"{p}{vp}GF_Form":      r[f"{vp}GF_Form"],
        f"{p}{vp}SOT_Form":     r[f"{vp}SOT_Form"],
        f"{p}Travel_Fatigue_5": r["Travel_Fatigue_5"],
    }

# Train final Poisson models on all available data
print("Training deployment Poisson Regression on full dataset...")
sc_deploy = StandardScaler()
X_all_sc  = sc_deploy.fit_transform(X)

pr_h_deploy = PoissonRegressor(alpha=0.1, max_iter=1000).fit(X_all_sc, df["FTHG"])
pr_a_deploy = PoissonRegressor(alpha=0.1, max_iter=1000).fit(X_all_sc, df["FTAG"])

# Build live feature matrix (column order must match FEATURES)
X_live = pd.DataFrame([
    {**get_latest_features(m["HomeTeam"], True),
     **get_latest_features(m["AwayTeam"], False)}
    for m in FINAL_WEEK
])[FEATURES].fillna(0)

X_live_sc = sc_deploy.transform(X_live)

# Calculate bivariate Poisson probabilities for live matches
live_preds = []
for lh, la in zip(pr_h_deploy.predict(X_live_sc), pr_a_deploy.predict(X_live_sc)):
    lh, la = max(float(lh), 1e-6), max(float(la), 1e-6)
    ph, pd_tie, pa = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
    for h in range(10):
        for a in range(10):
            ps = poisson.pmf(h, lh) * poisson.pmf(a, la)
            if h > a:    ph += ps
            elif h == a: pd_tie += ps
            else:        pa += ps
    tot = ph + pd_tie + pa
    live_preds.append((pa / tot, pd_tie / tot, ph / tot))

# Print predictions
print(f"\n--- Matchday 38 (2025/26) Predictions — Poisson Regression ---\n")
header = f"{'Fixture':<35} | {'Home %':>7} | {'Draw %':>7} | {'Away %':>7} | {'H Odds':>7} | {'D Odds':>7} | {'A Odds':>7}"
print(header)
print("-" * len(header))
for m, (pa, pd_tie, ph) in zip(FINAL_WEEK, live_preds):
    # Clamp to avoid division by zero in implied odds
    ph, pd_tie, pa = max(float(ph), 1e-4), max(float(pd_tie), 1e-4), max(float(pa), 1e-4)
    fixture = f"{m['HomeTeam']} vs {m['AwayTeam']}"
    print(
        f"{fixture:<35} | {ph*100:>6.1f}% | {pd_tie*100:>6.1f}% | {pa*100:>6.1f}% "
        f"| {1/ph:>7.2f} | {1/pd_tie:>7.2f} | {1/pa:>7.2f}"
    )

How the features hold up by season¶

The models above were evaluated on shuffled folds. A tougher check is whether the features hold up season by season, and forward in time. To keep the test about the features rather than the model, I ran it with a single transparent model: multinomial logistic regression on the 12 engineered features. Same data throughout: 1,130 matches across 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26 (43.2% home win, 32.4% away win, 24.4% draw).

seasonmatches5-fold CV accuracy5-fold CV log-loss
2023-243800.5001.042
2024-253800.4971.038
2025-263700.4651.076

The signal is stable across the first two seasons and dips slightly in 2025-26. A forward test, training on 2023-24 and 2024-25 and testing on 2025-26, gives accuracy 0.478 and log-loss 1.067, consistent with the cross-validation story: the features generalize forward in time, not just within shuffled folds.

What the model actually uses¶

Twelve features is a small enough set to ask which groups carry the signal. I dropped feature groups one at a time and re-ran 5-fold CV with the same logistic model:

feature setn features5-fold CV accuracy5-fold CV log-loss
all features120.5111.014
no travel fatigue100.5191.011
venue splits only40.5111.020
rolling form only60.4911.023
always home win00.432—
class priors00.348—

Two honest findings. First, the model clearly beats the naive baselines: 0.511 accuracy against 0.432 for always predicting the home team. Second, the travel fatigue features do not earn their keep for this model: dropping them improves both accuracy (0.519) and log-loss (1.011). They may help a different model, but here they add noise. The venue-split features alone match the full set on accuracy, which says home/away form splits are doing most of the work.

One caveat: this checks the features through one model (multinomial logistic), not the Poisson or gradient boosting models above, and ablation results can differ by model class. Draws remain the hard case: most of the error is home/draw and away/draw confusion. Script: analysis/season_and_ablation.py in the repo.

Takeaway¶

Public match history gets you close to the betting market but not past it. A simple Poisson model on twelve leakage-free form features scores 1.0250 against the market's 0.9639, and its probabilities are well calibrated. The complex models lose because football has too much randomness to fit, and the clearest limit is draws: the model never predicts one. Against a benchmark with more information than you have, close and honest beats fancy and overfit.
